opening.headline: This explains why a model accesses columns it should not read, using inheritance permissions and masking policies.
body: After granting read permission to the model pipeline, access to sensitive columns also occurs because the permission is inherited by lower objects.

In this class, we will sequentially examine Unity Catalog's authorization structure, row filters and column masks, tag-based ABAC policies, and distinguish the differences in grant locations affecting scope.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain Unity Catalog permissions, row filtering, column masking, and ABAC.
Effects can be distinguished based on the authorization location (catalog, schema, table).

screens.title: Reason why columns that the model should not read are being displayed
screens.lead: First, let's examine how data access incidents occur. Review the scene and identify the point at which permissions became broader.

paragraphs: The customer table contains columns necessary for model training as well as columns that the model should not read. Purchase amount and region are required, but the original email is not necessary.

The data team granted read access to the entire schema to enable the model pipeline to function. As a result, the pipeline read not only the required columns but also sensitive columns. The configuration was set only once, yet its impact affected all tables within the schema.

The reason is that permissions are inherited downward. A single assignment to an upper object affects all objects below it. Therefore, where permissions are granted determines exactly how far access is extended.

In this class, we explain Unity Catalog's authorization model, row filtering and column masking as control mechanisms at the row and column levels, and attribute-based access control (ABAC) applied broadly using tags, distinguishing the impacts based on where permissions are assigned.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: We have granted permissions, but if we only want to restrict access to certain values that should not be read, can permissions alone solve this? Keep this question in mind as you proceed.

visual.alt: In the customer table, columns needed and sensitive columns are distinguished, showing the model pipeline reading both.
labels: Grant SELECT to the entire schema

screens.outro: Having confirmed the context of the customer data example, let us now recall your own experience.

screens.title: Have you encountered issues caused by permission inheritance?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced giving folder sharing permissions to a parent folder, only to find all the child files become accessible?
items.answer: This is a common issue in file sharing. The property where permissions from an upper folder are inherited by lower items is convenient but can lead to unintended exposure. The permission inheritance in data platforms follows the same structure.

items.prompt: Is it convenient or risky that the same permissions are automatically applied to tables added later?
items.answer: Both are acceptable; while it is convenient that management items do not increase, it poses a risk because permissions are already assigned even if sensitive columns are present in newly created tables. Therefore, the grant location must be carefully determined.

items.prompt: Reading is allowed, but when I only want to access certain values, what methods are available?
items.answer: With permissions alone, there are only two options: opening or closing a table. To hide values while allowing read access, row- or column-level policies are required. We now examine the methods in the following screen.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the structure wherein permissions are granted, in order to answer the question that arises.

screens.title: Unity Catalog Permissions: Grantor and Hierarchy
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the process of granting permissions and inheritance one step at a time.

steps.title: Basic is inaccessible
steps.body: The reason this starting point is important is that newly created objects are initially closed. In Unity Catalog, users cannot access data at first. They must explicitly be granted the necessary permissions before they can read it. This can be viewed as an allowlist mechanism. Objects that have not been granted permissions to anyone are inaccessible to anyone other than their owner.

steps.title: Every object has a owner.
steps.body: Catalogs, schemas, and tables are secure objects that have owners. The owner has all permissions on the object and the authority to grant permissions to other principals.

steps.title: Who can grant it?
steps.body: The principals who can be granted permissions are the object owner, the owner of the catalog or schema containing the object, a user who has MANAGE permission on the object, or a metastore administrator. The more principals who are granted permission, the broader the management scope becomes, so it is essential to verify who can grant permissions on which objects. Additionally, owners inherently possess all permissions on their own objects without any separate grants, which means testing using an owner account may not reflect the actual experience of regular users. This point becomes particularly important when verifying masking later on.

steps.title: Three permissions required to read a table
steps.body: To read a table, the catalog's `USE CATALOG`, schema's `USE SCHEMA`, and table's `SELECT` must all be available. If the table only has `SELECT` and lacks upper-level permissions, the query will fail.

steps.title: Inheritance expands the scope of influence.
steps.body: Permissions granted to a parent object are inherited by child objects. If `SELECT` is granted at the catalog level, all schemas and tables within that catalog are affected; if granted at the schema level, only the tables within that schema are affected. The point of grant is equivalent to the scope of influence.

screens.outro: You cannot determine values based on permissions alone; instead, let's examine policies that modify results at query time.

screens.title: row filter and column mask: limitations at query time
screens.lead: Select the Status button to compare how query results differ when executed by analysts and administrators.

states.label: When analysts query
states.body: Even with the same table, analysts see results that have applied policies. A **row filter** evaluates a SQL UDF for each row, and rows that return FALSE are excluded from the result. A **column mask** returns a masked value instead of the original value, so an email appears obscured. Mask UDFs can accept values from other columns as inputs and behave differently based on various attributes. Only one mask can be applied to a single column. Analyst queries do not fail, and the difference from access denial is that only values change within a readable scope.

states.label: When the administrator queries
states.body: If a UDF is evaluated within the context of a policy condition and is determined to be part of a management group, the UDF returns the original value unchanged. For the same table and same query, the original email content is displayed. Since the policy applies at query time without modifying stored data, the results vary depending on the user, but the stored original data remains unchanged in all cases. At the table level, row filtering can be set using `ALTER TABLE` or masking can be configured using `ALTER COLUMN`, both managed by the table owner. In contrast, since the same query yields different results depending on the user's group membership, the policy must be verified from the perspective of a general user. Both row filtering and value masking policies can be used together—for example, to restrict visibility to rows specific to a region while also masking email content. However, since policy UDFs are evaluated for every query, it is advisable to keep them as simple as possible.

screens.outro: Now that you understand individual table policies, let's move on to the method of applying policies to multiple tables at once.

screens.title: ABAC: Apply once using tags and policies
screens.lead: When you select the highlighted sections below, the meaning of that portion will be displayed. Please click on each section one by one.

data.text: ABAC is a model that determines access by evaluating properties attached to objects. In Unity Catalog, The governed tag serves the attribute role. policies are attached to layers such as metadata store, catalog, schema, and table, and The property is automatically applied to objects that have the target property. policies support row filter and column mask policies. To create a Policy is automatically applied if the same tag exists, even if a new table is added. policy, the target object's MANAGE privilege or ownership and masking logic UDF's EXECUTE privilege is required.

marks.span: The governed tag serves the attribute role.
marks.note: A tag is simply an attribute that a policy evaluates. When you apply a tag to an email column, that column becomes the target of the policy.

marks.span: The property is automatically applied to objects that have the target property.
marks.note: A policy is applied if the same tag is present, without needing to set it individually per table. The layers to which a policy is applied range from the metastore down to the table level.

marks.span: Policy is automatically applied if the same tag exists, even if a new table is added.
marks.note: Consistent rules are applied to tables created later, reducing the occurrence of omissions caused by overlooking individual settings.

marks.span: MANAGE privilege or ownership and masking logic UDF's EXECUTE privilege
marks.note: Two permissions are required to create policies. Without either permission, no policy can be created. By granting policy creation permission to a limited number of users, you can prevent accidental changes to masking rules.

screens.outro: ABAC, as defined by NIST SP 800-162, is a method that evaluates the attributes of the subject, object, and environment to determine authorization. Let's now apply this to a practical example.

screens.title: Explanation Example 1: Masking the Email Column in Customer Data
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of masking the email column step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: The model learning team needs to read purchase amounts and locations, but there's no need to view the email body. The goal is to only mask the email content while leaving everything else unchanged.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify inheritance issues
steps.body: First, we verify how much access is currently granted to the given user. If the schema assigns `SELECT`, it ends up reading the email column due to inheritance. This stage concludes that permissions alone cannot distinguish between columns.

steps.title: Step 2: Apply column mask
steps.body: In the email column, a column mask is applied so that general groups see masked values while management groups see the original values. Read permissions remain unchanged, with only the values differing. The learning pipeline operates using masked values, so the model team's work is not interrupted. The mask UDF can condition on whether a user belongs to a particular group.

steps.title: Step 3: Apply in bulk via tag
steps.body: Applying a mask to each table individually leads to omissions as the number of tables increases. If multiple tables contain columns that follow the same rule, apply the governed tag and ABAC policy once to cover them all. Even if a new table is created, simply attaching the tag ensures the same policy is applied.

steps.title: Step 4: Verification Method
steps.body: Verification involves querying with a general group account to check whether masked values are returned. If you query with owner privileges, the original values might be displayed, preventing proper verification. Just as policy design, this verification habit is equally important.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: In this scenario, the most common mistake is to start with masks alone. The correct flow is to first define read scopes using permissions, then apply masks to hide values, and finally use tags to ensure consistency. Simply adding masks after granting overly broad permissions is merely a temporary workaround; instead, you should first review and reduce the grant location. For example, if this team only needs three tables, consider granting `SELECT` access only to those three tables rather than to the entire schema. Policies complement, but do not replace, grant locations.

screens.outro: We've analyzed one case; now let's compare how different placement positions can have varying effects.

screens.title: Explanation Example 2: Differentiation Based on Location of the Fault
screens.lead: Compare the scope affected when assigning the same read permission to different locations across various tabs.

tabs.label: Assigned in catalog
tabs.body: This is the broadest privilege. Assigning `SELECT` in the catalog affects all schemas and tables within, as well as any objects created afterward. While management is the simplest, it poses the highest risk of unintended exposure. Even if a schema currently contains no sensitive columns, the privilege remains in place and will automatically apply when another team later adds a sensitive table.

tabs.label: Schema assigned
tabs.body: This is an intermediate option. If granted to a schema, it only affects the tables within that schema, narrowing the scope. However, if tables containing sensitive columns are mixed within that schema, those columns remain accessible. Customer data scenarios directly fall into this category. In such cases, schema-level grants may appear to narrow the scope, yet they do not resolve column-level issues.

tabs.label: Assigned to table
tabs.body: This is the most restrictive location. When assigned to a table, it provides the highest precision. It is safe because only necessary tables are opened, but as the number of tables increases, the management overhead grows. Each time a new table is created, the required assignments must be re-established, increasing operational burden. Do not forget that permissions for the parent object, `USE`, are also required. This approach is most appropriate when the table is part of a predefined workflow, such as a model pipeline.

tabs.label: conclusion
tabs.body: By comparing the three positions, a clear baseline is established. No single position is optimal for all scenarios, as the balance point varies depending on data sensitivity, table count, and management resources. The upper position is easy to manage but carries a high exposure risk, while the lower position is safer but increases the number of management items. Sensitive columns are typically designed by lowering their access level or by complementing them with masking and ABAC policies. Grant read access at the lowest necessary level, and separate sensitive value controls into policies. This distinction serves as the decision criterion for today's case. When reviewing designs, this statement can be used as a checklist.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: In Unity Catalog, permissions are inherited from above to below, and the assignment location defines the scope of influence. To read a table, permissions at the catalog, schema, and table levels are all required.

Values that cannot be controlled solely by permissions are managed by row filter and column mask. Both policies modify the results based on user conditions at query time without altering the original data. To apply the same rules across multiple tables, use governed tags and ABAC policies for consistent enforcement.

Going back to the initial question, when you want to grant permissions but only wish to allow access to values rather than full permissions, you should lower the permission level and add policies. Permissions alone allow only the choice to open or close a table, but policies can allow reading while still controlling the values.

Finally, remember the order to verify when designing. First, grant read access to the required lowest-level objects; next, apply masks or row filters to sensitive values; and when the same rules repeat, ensure consistency using tags and ABAC.

glossary.def: This is the property that permissions granted to a parent object such as a catalog or schema are automatically applied to its child objects.
Row-level access control that evaluates each row using a UDF and excludes rows from the result where FALSE is returned.
A UDF-based control that replaces column values with the original or masked value and returns them. Attached to one column only.
This is a model that evaluates the governed tag, an attribute attached to an object, as a policy condition to determine access.
This is a privilege that allows management of object permissions and policies.

misconceptions.myth: SELECT is safe when applied only to tables.
misconceptions.fact: To read a table, you also need catalog and schema privileges, and privileges on a parent object are inherited by child objects. You must also consider the grant location.

misconceptions.myth: Masking replaces data with altered values for storage.
misconceptions.fact: The original is unchanged and the values returned vary depending on the user at query time.

misconceptions.myth: ABAC must be configured separately for each table.
misconceptions.fact: When tags and policies are applied to a layer, they are automatically applied to objects that share the same tag.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: Permissions are inherited and masking is applied conditionally.
Its location in Buje is precisely its area of influence.
Row filter and column mask modify the results at query time.
ABAC applies consistent policies broadly using tag-based rules.

closing.reflection: Within our organization, where are permissions assigned and are they appropriate for their respective levels?

checks.q: The user has only been granted SELECT privilege on a table and has no privileges on the catalog or schema. What happens when this user queries the table?
options: The catalog has no USE CATALOG and the schema has no USE SCHEMA, making it unreadable.
It is normally read since a TABLE SELECT is sufficient.
The parent object automatically reads on behalf of the owner's permissions.
Reading is possible, but all columns return masked values.
checks.explain: To read a table, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT are all required. Initially, access permission is not granted and must be explicitly assigned.

wrong.1: SELECT alone is insufficient to access the parent object.
wrong.2: Owner permissions are not automatically applied in place.
wrong.3: Masking is a result when policies are applied, and it is a different issue from insufficient permissions.

checks.intro: You have just learned the privileges required to read a table. Check the result when no object privilege is granted. This is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. If the upper object does not have USE privilege, the table can only be read through SELECT statements.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. The privileges required to read a table are inherited up to the parent object.

left: I want only rows that satisfy specific conditions to be displayed.
I want to display the email value in a masked format.
Want to apply rules collectively to columns across multiple tables that have the same tag
Read permission defined at the schema extends to subordinate tables.
checks.explain: Row restriction is a row filter, value masking is a column mask, tag-based bulk application is an ABAC policy, and permissions flowing from above to below is inheritance.
checks.intro: Choose the appropriate control measures for each scenario. Scores are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Correctly connected the appropriate means to each requirement scenario.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are out of sync. Check whether it's a row filtering, value masking, or applied across multiple tables.

checks.q: In a schema containing multiple tables with sensitive columns, what design approach is most appropriate to ensure that a model team only reads the columns they need?
options: Grant SELECT to the catalog to link all subsequently created objects at once.
If SELECT is specified in the schema, inheritance automatically distinguishes columns, which is sufficient.
Grants owner permissions to the model team so they can use them autonomously as needed.
Read access is granted to the lowest required object and sensitive values are controlled using masking or ABAC policies.
checks.explain: Exposure to unintended leaks increases when inheritance is used. It is typical to design with reading access restricted to the lowest necessary level and to isolate sensitive values via policy.

wrong.0: Catalog assignment exposes the widest scope of impact and poses the highest risk.
wrong.1: Inheritance propagates to the entire object below without distinguishing columns.
wrong.2: Owner privileges mean all privileges, contrary to the principle of least privilege.

checks.intro: Design a schema with sensitive columns mixed in, and choose the most appropriate approach. This is an unrecorded self-assessment.
checks.correctFeedback: Appropriate design. The separation of lowest-level assignment and policy is key.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This design either opens unnecessarily or fails to distinguish sensitive values. Please reconsider the assigned location and the role of the policy.
